promise: After this you can explain what a cache is, how entries expire and get evicted, and what can go wrong.

terms.definition: How long one request takes to get an answer, usually measured in milliseconds.
The authoritative source of the data, such as the database, which a cache sits in front of.
A cache stores a value under a key and hands it back when you ask for that key.

before.note: Read Load Balancing first, since a cache is one more stop in the request path. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: Some answers are expensive to compute or slow to fetch, and the same answer is asked for again and again. A cache keeps a copy of a recent answer close by so the next request can be served from the copy instead of redoing the work. RFC 9111 says an HTTP cache stores responses so that later equivalent requests are answered faster and use less bandwidth [[rfc9111]]. Memcached was first meant to take load off the database behind a dynamic web site, and its page suggests thinking of it as a short-term memory for an application [[memcached-about]].

The core idea is a key-value store held in memory. You look up a key; if the value is present that is a hit, and if it is absent that is a miss and you fall back to the origin, then usually store the result for next time. Memcached's page adds a point about clusters. If every web server keeps its own cache, fifty servers still give you only one server's 64MB of usable cache. If they pool their memory, the same fifty give 3.2GB, and any given item always lives in one place [[memcached-about]].

Because memory is limited and the origin can change, a cached copy is only a bet that the answer is still good and still worth keeping. Redis frames the memory side: cache entries are copies of persistently stored data, so it is usually safe to evict them when the cache runs out of memory, since they can be cached again later [[redis-eviction]]. That leaves two decisions to make for every cache: when a copy expires, and what to drop when memory is full.

stages.name: How it works
body: The common pattern is cache-aside: the application checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the origin, stores the result in the cache, and returns it. The cache does not know about the database; the application wires them together.

Entries do not live forever. Each can carry a time to live, after which it expires and the next lookup is a miss that refills it. A short time to live keeps data fresh but lowers the hit ratio; a long one does the opposite. This is the same freshness-versus-load trade-off that DNS caching had, now under your control per key. In Redis you can set one in the same command that stores the value, as the SET page shows with its EX option for a time to live in seconds [[redis-set]].

Memory fills up, so a cache needs an eviction policy to decide what to drop. Redis lets you set a memory limit with maxmemory and choose a policy with maxmemory-policy. The policies include evicting the least recently used keys (allkeys-lru), the least frequently used keys (allkeys-lfu) or keys at random (allkeys-random), and the volatile versions apply only to keys that have an expiration. With noeviction, keys are not evicted and the server returns an error when you try to cache new data [[redis-eviction]].

For HTTP responses the web has a shared, standard caching language. The Cache-Control header, with directives such as max-age, tells caches how long a response may be reused and whether it may be stored at all, and validators let a cache ask the origin "is my copy still good?" without refetching the whole thing [[rfc9111]].

terms.definition: The app checks the cache, and on a miss reads the origin and fills the cache itself.
How long a cached entry may be reused before it expires and must be refetched.
The rule for which entry to drop when the cache is full, such as least recently used.
The HTTP header that tells caches whether and how long a response may be stored.
A tag like an ETag that lets a cache check with the origin whether its copy is still current.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: The hardest part of caching is invalidation: when the origin changes, copies in the cache are now wrong until they expire or are removed. A short time to live limits how long a stale copy can live but costs hit ratio. Explicitly deleting the key on a write keeps data fresh but needs the write path to know every key it affects. RFC 9111 has a related rule: because unsafe methods such as PUT, POST or DELETE can change state on the origin, a cache must invalidate the stored responses for the target URI when it gets a non-error response to one [[rfc9111]]. It applies to the caches that see that exchange.
Our own explanation, not from a cited source: a stampede, also called a cache miss storm, is when a single hot key expires and many requests miss it at once and reach the origin together.

Eviction policy choice matters more than it looks. Redis's rule of thumb is to use allkeys-lru when a subset of elements will be accessed far more often than the rest, which it calls a very common case and a good default if you have no reason to prefer another, and allkeys-random when keys are accessed with roughly equal frequency. It also notes that the volatile versions of LRU and random are mainly useful when one instance serves both caching and persistent keys, and suggests two separate instances if possible [[redis-eviction]].

terms.definition: Removing or updating a cached copy once the origin's value has changed.
A cached value that no longer matches the origin.
Many requests missing the same expired key at once and all hitting the origin together.
Least recently used drops what has not been touched lately; least frequently used drops what is asked for least often.

reading.what: When a cache must invalidate stored responses, the standard form of explicit invalidation.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: Caching speeds reads at the cost of freshness. Every cache decision is really a choice about how stale an answer you can tolerate: a price page can be seconds old, a bank balance usually cannot. Setting the time to live and the invalidation strategy per kind of data, rather than one global rule, is what separates a cache that helps from one that serves wrong answers.

Caches also change failure modes. In our own words, not from a cited source: if the cache is down, requests that would have been hits go to the origin, so a cache the origin cannot live without has become part of the critical path. Redis shows how to check that the cache is helping: the INFO stats section reports keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses, and keyspace_hits / (keyspace_hits + keyspace_misses) * 100 gives the percentage of accesses served from the cache, which you compare with what you expect for your app [[redis-eviction]].

Where you cache matters as much as whether you do. RFC 9111 separates a shared cache, which reuses responses for more than one user and usually sits in an intermediary, from a private cache that serves a single user [[rfc9111]]. A cache close to the application cuts database load; a cache close to the user, at the edge, cuts network latency as well. That second idea, shared copies placed out in the network, is what CDNs do, which is why CDNs come right after caching on the map.

misconceptions.myth: Caching is free performance with no downside.
misconceptions.truth: It trades freshness for speed; a stored response can go stale, and RFC 9111 has a whole set of rules about freshness, validation and invalidation to manage that [[rfc9111]].

misconceptions.myth: A cache remembers everything you put in it.
misconceptions.truth: Memory is limited, so once you set a maxmemory limit Redis evicts keys by the chosen policy when it is reached (by default on 64-bit systems there is no limit), and with noeviction it returns an error instead of caching new data [[redis-eviction]].

misconceptions.myth: The cache keeps itself in sync with the database.
misconceptions.truth: A cache does not update itself. With cache-aside the application wires the cache and the database together, and a Redis cache entry is only a copy of data stored elsewhere [[redis-eviction]].

misconceptions.myth: A longer time to live is always better.
misconceptions.truth: A longer time to live raises the hit ratio but lets stale data live longer, so the right value depends on how fresh the data must be. Redis says that if evicted_keys is low and expired_keys is high, the TTL may be too low [[redis-eviction]].
